title: Laboratory Rearing and Infection Tracking of Rhodnius prolixus Using 3D-Printable Designs
author: Harrison, Etheridge

steps.title: Assemble disposable cardboard cage
steps.instruction: Prepare and assemble a high‑throughput disposable cage using a 32 oz deli cup, corrugated cardboard strips, a donut lid with medium‑fine nylon mesh, and follow cleaning guidelines.

substeps.instruction: Mark the edge of a corrugated cardboard roll every 9.5 cm using the ruler on a guillotine‑style cutter and cut to obtain several 9.5 cm × 23 cm rectangles (≈1 min per cage).
Cut each rectangle transversely to produce one 9.5 cm × 9.5 cm square and one 9.5 cm × 13.5 cm rectangle.
From the 9.5 cm × 9.5 cm square, cut a circle of ~7.5 cm diameter using a circle cutter or scissors.
Make a central vertical slit in each 9.5 cm × 13.5 cm rectangle with scissors.
Slot the two slitted rectangles together to form a cross‑shaped vertical support; trim the outer bottom corners and a V‑shaped indent at the top centre to improve fit inside the deli cup.

Assemble the cage: place the 7.5 cm cardboard circle at the bottom of the deli cup, insert the vertical cross‑shaped supports in the middle, and secure the commercially acquired donut lid (with medium‑fine nylon mesh sandwiched between its lower and upper halves) on top.

CRITICAL: Replace cages at least every 2 weeks or whenever heavily soiled. Freeze deli cups and cardboard pieces for 24 h to kill hidden insects/eggs before disposal. Soak donut lids and nylon mesh in 10 % bleach for 2–16 h, then rinse thoroughly before reuse.

steps.title: Print and assemble 3D‑printed cage
steps.instruction: Print, roughen, and assemble reusable 3D‑printed vertical supports and lid components with a disposable deli cup and filter paper, then follow density and cleaning recommendations.

substeps.instruction: Print the lower and upper vertical support pieces (30 min – 1 h 30 min each) and the lid components (upper, lower, washer, clamps; 30 min – 1 h 30 min each) using regular plastic filament or, optionally, silver‑nanoparticle filament for antimicrobial effect (total 3–5 h per cage).
Roughen the surface of each printed support with coarse‑grain sandpaper to improve climbing ability of early‑stage nymphs.

Place a 7.5 cm diameter filter‑paper circle (or equivalent Aeropress filter) on the bottom of the deli cup, insert the two vertical supports in the centre, and position the 3D‑printed lid pieces with medium‑fine nylon mesh sandwiched between the lower and upper halves.
Secure the lid by placing the washer around the outside of the cup rim and tightening the three clamps around the washer and lid pieces.

Recommended rearing densities per 32 oz deli cup: 1st instar eggs – no upper limit (minimum 250); 2nd instar – 100–300; 3rd instar – 50–100; 4th instar – 50; 5th instar – 50; adults – 50 (ensure 18–20 females among adults for high egg yield).
For adult oviposition on 3D‑printed supports, add craft‑style pipe cleaners inside the cage as a substrate for egg attachment.

CRITICAL: Change cages at least every 2 weeks or when excessively soiled. Freeze deli cups and filter paper for 24 h before disposal. Clean 3D‑printed supports, lid pieces, and nylon mesh by soaking in 10 % bleach for 2–16 h, then rinse thoroughly before reuse.

Note: Mixed‑stage housing is possible but separate‑stage cages simplify husbandry; transfer eggs by moving pipe cleaners with adhered eggs to a new cage, allow hatching, then blood‑feed nymphs en masse before reducing density.

steps.title: Prepare balloon‑handwarmer feeder
steps.instruction: Construct an inexpensive artificial membrane feeding system using water balloons, electric handwarmers, and a 3D‑printed adapter; supplement blood as indicated.

substeps.instruction: Trim the straw to the appropriate length, pull a latex water balloon onto the straw tip, and secure it with a small rubber band (do not remove the band completely).

Load a syringe with 2.5–10 ml of anticoagulated (heparin) or defibrinated sheep blood (mechanically defibrinated to prevent clotting). Volumes <2.5 ml do not stretch the balloon sufficiently; >10 ml may heat unevenly.

Attach the balloon‑filled straw to the syringe tip, gently dispense blood into the balloon, then pinch the balloon above the straw, pull it off, and seal the end with the rubber band; optionally tie a knot for extra security.
Place an electric handwarmer into the 3D‑printed adapter, clamp the balloon’s knotted end into the adapter hole, and stretch the knot into the cavity so the balloon is held securely.
Activate the handwarmer, invert the assembled feeder, and position it atop the cage lid. Apply a thin coat of Vaseline to the balloon surface to prevent it from sticking to the nylon mesh.
Supplement the blood with Rhodococcus rhodnii at a final concentration of 1 × 10⁶ CFU ml⁻¹ to support colony health, especially when using silver‑nanoparticle printed supports.
If large‑stage insects (4th/5th instars or starved adults) drain the balloon before all individuals feed, prepare a second filled balloon and swap it in to allow complete feeding.

steps.title: Purify T. cruzi via OptiPrep gradient
steps.instruction: Isolate Trypanosoma cruzi from insect excreta or gut homogenate using a two‑layer iodixanol (OptiPrep) density gradient and collect the parasite‑rich fraction.

substeps.instruction: Prepare sterile 6 % (v/v) OptiPrep and 20 % OptiPrep solutions in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle’s Medium (DMEM) containing 15 % heat‑inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS). Store at 4 °C and keep on ice during gradient preparation. Ensure serum concentration is 10–15 % to prevent epimastigotes from adhering to tube walls.
Pellet the sample (excreta or gut homogenate) by centrifugation at 1 000 × g for 10 min at 4 °C.

For gut homogenate: place a dissected whole gastrointestinal tract or only the hindgut into a 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tube with 400 µl sterile PBS, then macerate with a sterile pestle or bead homogenizer.
Discard the supernatant and resuspend the pellet in 2 ml of 20 % OptiPrep; keep this suspension on ice.
Add 2 ml of 6 % OptiPrep to a 15 ml conical tube kept on ice.
Slowly layer the 2 ml sample (20 % OptiPrep) beneath the 6 % layer by gently advancing the pipette tip just under the interface, avoiding any mixing of the two layers.
Centrifuge the gradient at 3 400 × g for 30 min at 4 °C in a pre‑chilled bucket‑rotor; set deceleration to low or zero to prevent layer disturbance.
Using a pipette, carefully draw 500 µl of the 6 % layer immediately above the 6 %–20 % interface, moving the tip in a circular motion to collect trypanosomes from the entire interface surface.
Transfer the 500 µl trypanosome‑containing fraction to a new sterile tube for downstream microscopy, cultivation, or other applications.

description: Insects belonging to the subfamily Triatominae, commonly referred to as triatomines or kissing bugs are primarily hematophagous and can subsist on blood alone throughout the entire duration of their lifespan.1 Triatomines require blood meals to progress through successive stages of juvenile development, for subsistence as adults and, in the case of adult females, for egg formation.2 This blood-feeding habit underlies the triatomine ability to acquire and transmit the deadly parasite Trypanosoma cruzi to vertebrate hosts including humans. Infection with this parasite can lead to Chagas disease, endemic to the Americas, which infects an estimated 6–7 million people and causes approximately 12,000 deaths each year.3 Elucidating how T. cruzi establishes infection within triatomines is crucial for developing novel strategies to disrupt ongoing transmission in endemic areas. A barrier for rearing triatomines is provisioning this all-blood diet. To date, no artificial diet has been developed for triatomines, and use of animals for insect colony maintenance requires approval and continual update of animal use protocols, an animal care facility, associated training and reagents for anesthesia, and raises ethical concerns.4 Further, triatomines consume large amounts of blood corresponding to volumes as high as 400 μl per individual depending on species and life stage,5,6 which would rapidly lead to exsanguination of small mammals if a large number of insects were allowed to feed. The use of a membrane feeding system with commercially available sources of blood mitigates several of these problems but requires equipment that may not be accessible to all due to economic or other factors.
